extracted.intended_audience: general public and stakeholders interested in net neutrality and the federal rulemaking/public-comment process
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and criteria for assessing the trustworthiness and integrity of public comments submitted to regulatory agencies (illustrated by the FCC net-neutrality proceeding). Focuses on authenticity, duplication, provenance, and whether the record is suitable for a legitimate vote.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity of commenters
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether comments come from genuine, unique individuals versus fabricated identities or automated accounts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pew found many comments were duplicated or came from non-person names (e.g., 'The Internet'); the presence of obviously fake names undermines trust in the comment corpus. Verify uniqueness of submitters and look for markers of fabricated identities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duplicate / multiple submissions
rubrics_metrics.description: Extent to which the same comment text or the same submission is filed multiple times.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pew reported 94% of the comments 'were submitted multiple times, and in some cases those comments were submitted many hundreds of thousands of times.' High duplication often indicates organized mass campaigns rather than independent public input.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevalence of identical/template comments
rubrics_metrics.description: How many comments are identical or follow a small set of common templates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The most prevalent single comment was filed 2.8 million times and the next six most prevalent favored the opposite view; large numbers of identical comments suggest form letters or automated campaigns and reduce the evidentiary weight of raw comment counts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anomalous timing patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether large numbers of comments arrive at the exact same timestamp or in bursts inconsistent with organic submissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pew observed tens of thousands of comments arriving at the same precise moment—such timing anomalies are a sign of automation or scripted submission and should trigger further scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provenance / email-origin and geography
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether comment-origin information (email addresses, IPs) indicates foreign or suspicious sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Democratic Commissioner Rosenworcel said half a million fake comments originated from Russian email addresses; identifying origins can reveal foreign influence or bot networks and inform decisions about record reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Name anomalies and duplications
rubrics_metrics.description: Patterns in the names attached to comments, including repeated common names or non-name values.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pew noted many duplicates and entries that were not personal names (e.g., 'The Internet') and even high-profile names appearing in large numbers (John Oliver). Check for implausible name distributions (many 'John Smith' entries, celebrity names) as red flags.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organized campaign vs. individual submissions
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguishing coordinated advocacy campaigns from independently submitted public commentary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organized campaigns to influence policy are common, but the scale and automation here ('almost all of the comments seem to have been parts of organized campaigns') matters; agencies should account for coordinated drives when interpreting comment totals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrity of the rulemaking record
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the administrative record is reliable and coherent enough to support a legitimate rulemaking decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As New York AG Schneiderman stated, 'You cannot conduct a legitimate vote on a rule-making proceeding if you have a record that is in shambles as this one is.' If the record contains massive fraud or manipulation, its integrity—and the legitimacy of a vote—may be compromised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for investigation when record is compromised
rubrics_metrics.description: When and whether to pause or delay decision-making to investigate suspected fraud in the comment record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Calls from Schneiderman, Commissioner Rosenworcel, and multiple senators urged delaying the FCC vote to investigate fraudulent comments. If evidence shows substantial manipulation, agencies should consider formal investigations before final action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public transparency and verification tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Providing public-facing means for individuals to check whether their names/comments appear in the record and to understand the composition of submissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schneiderman set up a website to let people see if their names appear on comments—agencies and investigators should publish searchable tools and datasets so individuals and researchers can verify and audit the record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Managing comment integrity in the digital age
rubrics_metrics.description: The obligation for agencies to develop methods and policies to preserve the integrity of public input in an era of automated/online submissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rosenworcel emphasized 'it is essential that we come up with ways to manage the integrity of that process in the digital age.' Guidance includes adopting verification protocols, anomaly-detection, rate-limiting, authentication measures, and policies for weighting or excluding mass/submitted-form comments.
